segments: 293 and saying,
that they had nothing in the chest of the monks,
and they opened it in the church of the Franks.
Suddenly, there was a violent shock,
and dark clouds covered the air,
and bitter hail beat down,
and the streets were filled with it.
And all the people began to cry out:
"Kyrie eleison,
have mercy upon us,
O Chosen One of God!"
The Greeks, however, fled and hid themselves.
And when the hail ceased,
all the people gathered,
and they made supplication for three days.
And the zealots, the people of Harran, when they saw the wonder,
demanded that the Right Hand should also go to them.
The Franks, however, did not allow it,
but returned it with honor to the monastery.
And the people of Melitene came
and carried the Right Hand to their city with services and songs.
And at that time the mouth of the locust was bound,
and it did not harm the crops at all.
And on the twenty-third, lightning burned {OCR?} one Turk.
And in Armenia there was a severe earthquake,
and the city of Dogodaph fell.
And in Melitene there was a harsh winter,
and red snow fell.
And in the year one thousand four hundred and forty-six
— 1446 of the Greeks (1135 of our Lord?) —
a certain Frankish man whose name was Bedwi (Raymond of Poitiers?) set out from Italy,
and he took to wife the daughter of Bohemond, lord of Antioch,
the one who was killed,
in marriage,
and he reigned over Antioch.
And in that same year died Baldwin (the Second?), king of Jerusalem,
and a man named Foug (Fulk?) took his daughter in marriage
over Jerusalem.
And in that same year, which was the year five hundred and twenty-nine
— 529 of the Arabs —
Zengi, lord of Mosul, sent his son to Baghdad,
and with him the keys of Mosul,
and also noble women of his own.
And he swore and promised submission,
and he was received with honor.
And the Caliph also became reconciled with Sultan Sanjar,
and he sent him a crown, a collar, and a horse shod with shoes of gold.
And Sanjar arose and kissed the hooves of the horse,
and said:
"I am a servant and a subject."
And at that time the Catholicos of the Nestorians, who was called Bar Gabbara,
when he went out at night into the garden,
trod upon a snake,
and it bit him,
and he died.
And some say
that he was not bitten,
but rather died of fright.
And in that year,
